sections.h: Prisoner and witness: Caesarea to Rome
sections.b: Acts 24–28 follows Paul through two years of custody in Caesarea under Felix, a hearing before Festus, his appeal to Caesar, his defense before Agrippa II and Bernice, a shipwreck on Malta, and two years under guard in Rome. In every hearing he presents himself as a loyal Jew and a Pharisee, on trial for Israel's hope of the resurrection (Acts 24:14–15; 26:4–8; 28:20). His third account of his call (Acts 26:9–18) has Jesus commission him directly, in the language of the prophets' calls. Roman officials repeatedly find nothing worth death or chains (Acts 25:25; 26:31–32). Acts ends with Paul preaching "unhindered" in Rome and does not tell his fate; early tradition places his death there under Nero (1 Clement 5:5–7; Eusebius, Church History 2.22, 2.25), and some sources say he was first released and traveled west.

common: Most scholars accept that Paul was held in Caesarea and then taken to Rome as a prisoner, and that he died in Rome in the 60s.
uncommon: Some think Paul was released after the two years of Acts 28:30, preached in Spain, and was arrested again before his death; others think he died at the end of those two years.

sections.b: Acts closes with Paul in Rome, under guard in his own lodging for two whole years, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ, "and no one stopped him" (Acts 28:31). It does not tell the result of his appeal or his death. Explanations: Luke wrote before the outcome (about 62); Luke knew of Paul's death, foreshadowed in Acts 20:25, 38, but chose to end on the triumph of the word; Luke planned a third volume; or the open ending invites readers to carry the story on. The last scene with Rome's Jews (Acts 28:17–28), with Isaiah 6 and the turn to the Gentiles, is the key text for how Luke-Acts sees Israel's future.
sections.refs: Acts 1:8; Acts 20:25; Acts 20:38; Acts 23:11; Acts 28:17–31; Isaiah 6:9–10

sections.b: Acts 24–26 is the fullest picture in the New Testament of a Roman provincial trial: a formal accusation by a hired advocate (Acts 24:1–8), the defendant's reply, an adjournment and custody with privileges (Acts 24:22–23), a governor hoping for a bribe (Acts 24:26), a new governor's consultation with his council, and a citizen's appeal to the emperor (Acts 25:11–12). The charge that counted was sedition: Paul was called a plague who stirred up riots across the world (Acts 24:5). Roman officials repeatedly find no crime (Acts 25:25; 26:31–32), and the appeal brings Paul to Rome, the goal Jesus set in Acts 23:11. A. N. Sherwin-White judged the legal details accurate for the 50s and 60s.

Facing a transfer to Jerusalem and an ambush, Paul uses his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to the emperor (Acts 25:9–12). He grants that a crime worth death should be punished, "I am not trying to get out of dying" (Acts 25:11), but refuses to be handed over as a political favor. The episode has been cited by Christians as a model for using the protections of law and citizenship with a clear conscience. Luke also shows the limits of Roman justice: Felix delays and hopes for a bribe, and both Felix and Festus try to please the Jerusalem leaders (Acts 24:26–27; 25:9).

The last generation of Herods appears in Acts 24–26. Drusilla, daughter of Agrippa I, left her husband King Azizus of Emesa to marry the governor Felix (Josephus, Antiquities 20.141–144), and with him heard Paul speak of self-control and judgment (Acts 24:24–25). Her brother Agrippa II, who controlled the temple and its high priests, and their sister Bernice heard Paul's longest defense (Acts 25:13–26:32). Agrippa answered with irony, "With so little, you would talk me into making myself a Christian?" (Acts 26:28), but judged Paul innocent. Bernice later became the companion of Titus, who destroyed Jerusalem.

sections.h: "The resurrection of the dead" as Paul's defense
sections.b: In every hearing of Acts 23–28 Paul says the real issue is the resurrection: "I am being judged by you today over the resurrection of the dead!" (Acts 24:21). He tells Felix he shares with his accusers the hope "that a resurrection is coming, of the righteous and the unrighteous alike" (Acts 24:15), the only place Paul mentions the raising of the unrighteous. Festus summarizes the case as a dispute about "one Jesus, who had died, and who Paul kept saying is alive" (Acts 25:19), and Paul asks Agrippa why anyone should find it beyond belief "that God raises dead people" (Acts 26:8). Jesus is "the first one raised out of death" (Acts 26:23).

common: Christians have read Acts 24:15 as evidence that all the dead, good and bad, will be raised for judgment.
uncommon: Jehovah's Witnesses read "the unrighteous" in Acts 24:15 as people who never knew God's ways and will be raised to an earthly opportunity during the thousand years.

sections.h: Paul's last word to the Jews of Rome
sections.b: Acts ends with Paul calling the leaders of Rome's Jewish community "brothers" and saying he wears his chain "on account of Israel's hope" (Acts 28:17–20). After a day of teaching, some are persuaded and some refuse (Acts 28:24). Paul applies Isaiah 6:9–10 to those who refuse and announces that God's salvation "has been sent out to the Gentiles. They will listen" (Acts 28:28). Scholars disagree whether this is Luke's final verdict on the Jewish people (Jack T. Sanders, Haenchen), a picture of a divided Israel whose believing part is the restored people (Jervell), or an open tragedy (Tannehill). The passage was long used to teach that God had rejected the Jews, a teaching many churches have since rejected.
sections.refs: Acts 13:46–48; Acts 18:6; Acts 28:17–31; Isaiah 6:9–10; Romans 11:1–2; Romans 11:25–29

sections.b: In Acts 25 Festus speaks of the emperor (Nero) with the titles of imperial honor: Sebastos, the Greek form of "Augustus," "the revered one" (Acts 25:21, 25), and simply "the lord" (Acts 25:26). The cohort that escorts Paul is also "Augustan" (Acts 27:1). Augustus and Tiberius had refused to be called "master," but by Nero's time "lord" was common in the Greek East, and Domitian later wanted to be called "lord and god." Christians used the same word, kyrios, in confessing "Jesus is Lord," a confession that brought them into conflict with the emperor's cult in the next century.
sections.refs: Acts 25:21; Acts 25:25–26; Acts 27:1; Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 8:5–6; Revelation 13:4

sections.b: Before Agrippa, Paul says all the Jews know that he lived as a Pharisee, following "the most exacting party of our religion" (Acts 26:5); earlier he had said in the present tense, "I am a Pharisee" (Acts 23:6). The word for "exacting" is the one Josephus uses for the Pharisees' reputation for precise interpretation of the law. Paul's letters agree (Philippians 3:5; Galatians 1:14). He is the only Pharisee from before AD 70 whose own writings survive, which makes him an important witness for Jewish scholars studying the period.

Luke dates Paul's voyage by the Jewish calendar: by Fair Havens "the Fast was already past" (Acts 27:9). The Day of Atonement fell on the tenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29; 23:27), in September or October, near the close of the safe sailing season, which the Roman writer Vegetius ended in mid-September and closed entirely from 11 November. In the first century the day was known simply as "the Fast," the one fast the Law commanded.

Acts 27 is the Bible's longest sea story: a voyage from Caesarea toward Rome, a northeaster off Crete, fourteen days adrift across the Adria, and a wreck on Malta. Its sailing details have been checked by sailors and historians since James Smith (1848). The story echoes Jonah 1 (a storm, cargo thrown out, a servant of God who names his God to pagan sailors) and the psalm of those who go down to the sea in ships (Psalm 107:23–30). God's promise through Paul that no life would be lost (Acts 27:22–25) makes the sea, again, a place where God shows his rule over chaos.

On Malta Paul visits the father of Publius, sick with fevers and dysentery, prays, lays his hands on him and heals him; then the island's other sick come and are cured (Acts 28:8–9). The scene echoes Jesus healing Peter's mother-in-law of a fever and then the crowds at sunset (Luke 4:38–40), one of many places where Acts mirrors the Gospel. It is the last healing in Acts. Christians differ on whether such gifts continue (see the card at Acts 28).

Paul's last journey is marked by hospitality: friends in Sidon care for him (Acts 27:3); the non-Greek-speaking Maltese welcome 276 shipwrecked strangers who were kind to them "beyond the ordinary" (Acts 28:2); Publius hosts them for three days (Acts 28:7); believers in Puteoli keep them a week, and Roman believers walk out along the Appian Way to meet them (Acts 28:14–15). In Rome Paul in turn welcomes everyone who comes to his lodging (Acts 28:30).

sections.h: The kingdom of God at the end of Acts
sections.b: Acts begins with the risen Jesus teaching about the kingdom of God for forty days (Acts 1:3) and ends with Paul in Rome testifying to the kingdom of God from morning to evening (Acts 28:23) and proclaiming it for two years (Acts 28:31). The kingdom frames the whole book. In between it is preached by Philip and Paul (Acts 8:12; 14:22; 19:8; 20:25).

sections.b: Luke's Gospel quotes only a few words of Isaiah 6:9–10 (Luke 8:10) and saves the full quotation for the last scene of Acts, where Paul applies it to Rome's Jews who refuse his message (Acts 28:26–27). The Greek, as in Matthew 13:14–15, says the people's heart "has become sluggish," their own doing, where the Hebrew has God tell the prophet to make it so. The quotation ends with a future verb, "and I will heal them," which some read as a door left open.
sections.refs: Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:39–40; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 11:7–8

sections.b: In Paul's account of his call before Agrippa, Jesus sends him "to open their eyes, so they turn back from darkness to light" (Acts 26:18), the mission of Isaiah's servant, "a light to the nations" (Isaiah 42:6), sent "to open blind eyes" (Isaiah 42:7). Paul then says the Messiah, raised from the dead, "was going to announce light to the people and to the Gentiles" (Acts 26:23), echoing Isaiah 49:6, which Paul and Barnabas had applied to themselves at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:47). In Acts the servant's mission belongs to the Messiah and is carried on by his witnesses.
sections.refs: Isaiah 42:6–7; Isaiah 42:16; Isaiah 49:6; Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47; Acts 26:16–18; Acts 26:23

sections.b: Paul tells Agrippa that Moses and the prophets foretold "that the Messiah was to suffer, and that he, the first one raised out of death, was going to announce light" (Acts 26:23). The Greek may be a list of debated questions Paul argued from Scripture. A suffering Messiah was not the common expectation: the Targum of Isaiah calls the servant of Isaiah 52:13 "my servant the Messiah" but gives the suffering of Isaiah 53 to others. Luke's risen Jesus had made the same claim from Moses and the Prophets (Luke 24:26–27, 44–46).

sections.h: Two missing verses and the Western text in Acts 24–28
sections.b: Two verses printed in the King James Version are absent from the oldest manuscripts: Acts 24:7 (with parts of 24:6 and 24:8), in which Tertullus complains that the commander Lysias took Paul away by force, and Acts 28:29, in which the Jews leave Rome arguing. The first is not even in most Byzantine manuscripts; it entered the KJV through Erasmus' printed Greek. Codex Bezae, the chief Western manuscript of Acts, breaks off in Acts 22, so for these chapters the Western readings come from other witnesses such as minuscule 614, the Harclean Syriac and the Old Latin: the "camp commander" of Acts 28:16, "in fifteen days" at Acts 27:5, and "Away with our enemy!" at Acts 28:19.
sections.refs: Acts 24:6–8; Acts 27:5; Acts 27:37; Acts 28:16; Acts 28:19; Acts 28:29

sections.h: Acts 28:28 and the teaching of rejection
sections.b: Paul's last words in Acts, applying Isaiah's hardening to those who refused and announcing that God's salvation "has been sent out to the Gentiles" (Acts 28:28), were read for centuries as God's final rejection of the Jewish people. The passage itself describes a divided audience, "Some were persuaded by his words" (Acts 28:24), and Paul calls them "brothers" and wears his chain for "Israel's hope" (Acts 28:17, 20). Since 1965 (Nostra Aetate 4) the Catholic Church, and many Protestant churches, have rejected the reading that God has cast off the Jews, citing Romans 11:1–2 and 11:28–29.

sections.h: "I am not trying to get out of dying"
sections.b: Before Festus Paul says that if he has done something worth the death penalty, he does not refuse to die (Acts 25:11). Defenders of capital punishment have cited the verse, with Romans 13:4, as apostolic acceptance of the state's power of the sword; others answer that Paul is simply speaking as a defendant within Roman law and that the verse decides nothing about whether Christians should support executions.

Paul tells Felix he came to Jerusalem "to give alms for my people and to present offerings" (Acts 24:17). It is the only hint in Acts of the great collection from his Gentile churches for the poor of Jerusalem, which his letters describe at length (Romans 15:25–31; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Why Luke says so little about it is unexplained; some think the gift was refused or became entangled in Paul's arrest.
